EXPOSÉ IX
CONSTRUCTIBLE SHEAVES
COHOMOLOGY OF AN ALGEBRAIC CURVEby M. Artin
Contents

0. Introduction
1. The sorites of torsion sheaves
2. Constructible sheaves
3. Kummer and Artin-Schreier theories
4. The case of an algebraic curve
5. The trace method.
0. Introduction

It will be noted that, starting from the present exposé, in contrast to the preceding exposés and to the classical cohomological theory of topological spaces, we are obliged, for the validity of the essential statements, to restrict ourselves to torsion sheaves (and often even, more precisely, to torsion sheaves prime to the residue characteristics).

Let us point out that in fact a "reasonable" theory of cohomology with integer (or even real) coefficients, for varieties over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p \neq 0\), analogous to the classical theory in the case \(k = \mathbb{C}\), does not exist (as Serre has observed). More precisely, there does not exist a contravariant functor \(H^1\), defined say on the category of smooth projective schemes over the field \(K\) algebraically closed of characteristic \(p > 0\), with values in the category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over \(\mathbb{R}\) (or a subfield of \(\mathbb{R}\)), "commuting with products", i.e. such that \(H^1(X \times Y) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^1(X) \times H^1(Y)\), and such that \(\dim H^1(X) = 2\) if \(X\) is a connected curve of genus \(1\). Indeed, it would follow that if \(X\) is an abelian variety over \(k\), then the map \(u \mapsto u^1\) from \(\operatorname{End}(X)\) to \(\operatorname{End}(H^1(X))\) is additive, hence a representation of the opposite ring of \(\operatorname{End}(X)\). But in characteristic \(p\), there exist elliptic curves \(X\) whose endomorphism ring is a maximal order \(A\) of a quaternion algebra defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\) ([3], p.198), and such an algebra evidently has no representation in a vector space of dimension 2 over \(\mathbb{R}\), since \(A \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R}\) is a field (the field of quaternions).
1. The sorites of torsion sheaves

Let \(T\) be a topos and \(F\) an abelian sheaf on \(T\). One can multiply by \(n\) in \(F\) (\(n \in \mathbb{Z}\) an integer), this multiplication being induced by the analogous operation in \((\mathrm{Ab})\). We denote by \({}_n F\) the kernel of this multiplication; thus \({}_n F(X)\), for \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} T\), is the group of sections of \(F(X)\) whose order divides \(n\).
We denote by \(\mathbb{P}\) the set of all prime numbers.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

Let \(p\) be a set of prime numbers. We say that \(F\) is a \(p\)-torsion sheaf, or a \(p\)-sheaf, if the canonical morphism \[ \varinjlim_n {}_n F \longrightarrow F \quad \text{is bijective} , \] \(n\) ranging over the set of integers such that ass \(n \subset p\), that is, such that the prime numbers dividing \(n\) lie in \(p\). If \(p = \mathbb{P}\) is the set of all prime numbers, we say simply that \(F\) is torsion.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2

(i) \(F\) is \(p\)-torsion if and only if \(F\) is the sheaf associated to a presheaf with values in \(p\)-torsion abelian groups; one may take \[ P = \varinjlim_{\text{ass } n \subset p}^{(\text{préf})} {}_n F . \]

(ii) If \(F\) is \(p\)-torsion and if \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} T\) is a quasi-compact object(∗), then \(F(X)\) is a \(p\)-torsion group.

(iii) If \(T\) is locally of finite type (VI 1.1), then \(F\) is \(p\)-torsion if and only if \(F(X)\) is a \(p\)-torsion group for each \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} T\) quasi-compact. In this case, one has \[ \varinjlim_{\text{ass } n \subset p} H^q(T/X; {}_n F) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^q(T/X; F) \] for each \(X\) quasi-compact and every \(q\).

(iv) If \(u : T \to T'\) is a morphism of topoi and if \(F'\) is \(p\)-torsion on \(T'\), then the inverse image \(u^* F'\) is a \(p\)-torsion sheaf on \(T\).

(v) If \(u : T \to T'\) is a morphism of topoi, with \(T\) and \(T'\) locally of finite type and \(u\) quasi-compact(∗), and if \(F\) is a \(p\)-torsion sheaf on \(T\), then the \(R^q u_* F'\) are \(p\)-torsion sheaves on \(T\) for every \(q\).

Proof: (i) Evidently, if a sheaf \(F\) is \(p\)-torsion, \(F\) is the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(P\) whose group of sections \(P(X)\) is the subgroup of \(p\)-torsion elements of \(F(X)\). Conversely, let \(F = \underline{a} P\) (II) be the sheaf associated to \(P\), where \(P\) has values in the category of \(p\)-torsion abelian groups. From the exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow {}_n P \longrightarrow P \xrightarrow{\ n\ } P \] one deduces an exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow \underline{a}({}_n P) \longrightarrow F \xrightarrow{\ n\ } F , \] whence \(\underline{a}({}_n P) = {}_n F\). Since the functor \(\underline{a}\) commutes with inductive limits, one deduces from \[ \varinjlim_{\text{ass } n \subset p}^{(\text{préf})} {}_n P \xrightarrow{\sim} P \] that one also has \[ \varinjlim_{\text{ass } n \subset p} {}_n F \xrightarrow{\sim} F . \]

(ii) Set \(P = \varinjlim^{(\text{préf})} {}_n F\). Then one has \(P \subset F\), so \(P\) is a separated presheaf, and consequently \[ \underline{a} P(X) = \varinjlim \left( \ker\left( \textstyle\prod_i P(X_i) \rightrightarrows \right) \right) , \] where as usual the limit is taken over the covering families \(\{ X_i \longrightarrow X \}\). But since \(X\) is quasi-compact, it suffices to take the finite covering families. For these families \(\prod_i P(X_i)\) is \(p\)-torsion; hence the \(\ker\) is as well. Consequently \(\underline{a} P(X) = F(X)\) is \(p\)-torsion.

(iii) To verify that \(\varinjlim_n {}_n F \longrightarrow F\) is bijective, it suffices to do so for the values on \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} T\) for each \(X\) in a family of generators. One is thus reduced to (ii) for the first assertion. The second assertion is a consequence of
(iv) Consequence of (i) since \(u^*(\underline{a} P') = \underline{a}(u' P)\)
(v) Easy consequence of (iii).

We shall also need a non-abelian variant. But there are technical problems in the definition (I do not know whether they are serious), and we shall therefore content ourselves with giving a definition for the étale topology of a scheme.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.3

Let \(p\) be a set of prime numbers. We say that a group \(G\) is an ind-\(p\)-group if every finite subset of \(G\) generates a finite subgroup of order \(n\), with ass \(n \subset p\). It amounts to the same to say that the finite subgroups \(G_\alpha\) of order \(n_\alpha\), with ass \(n_\alpha \subset p\), form a filtered set, and that \(G = \varinjlim G_\alpha\). If \(p = \mathbb{P}\), we say ind-finite group instead of ind-\(p\)-group.
One verifies immediately the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.4

(i) A subgroup, as well as a quotient, of an ind \(p\)-group is again an ind \(p\)-group.

(ii) A filtered inductive limit of ind-\(p\)-groups is an ind-\(p\)-group.

(iii) A finite projective limit of ind-\(p\)-groups is an ind-\(p\)-group.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.5

Let \(X\) be a scheme. We say that a sheaf \(F\) of groups on \(X\) is a sheaf of ind-\(p\)-groups (resp. of ind-finite groups) if for each \(U \longrightarrow X\) étale, with \(U\) quasi-compact, \(F(U)\) is an ind \(p\)-group (resp. an ind-finite group).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.6

Let \(F\) be a sheaf of groups on the scheme \(X\).

(i) \(F\) is a sheaf of ind-\(p\)-groups if and only if for each geometric point \(\xi\) of \(X\), the stalk \(F_\xi\) is an ind-\(p\)-group.

(ii) If \(f : X \longrightarrow X'\) is a morphism and if \(F'\) is a sheaf of ind-\(p\)-groups on \(X'\), \(f^* F'\) is a sheaf of ind-\(p\)-groups.

(iii) If \(f : X \longrightarrow X'\) is a quasi-compact morphism and \(F\) is a sheaf of ind-\(p\)-groups on \(X\), then \(f_* F\) is a sheaf of ind-\(p\)-groups.

Proof. (i) Suppose that \(F\) is a sheaf of ind-\(p\)-groups, and let \(\xi\) be a geometric point of \(X\). Then \(F = \varinjlim F(X')\), where \(X'\) ranges over a pseudo-filtered system of schemes étale over \(X\) (VIII 3.9). It is evident that the affine (hence quasi-compact) \(X'\) form a cofinal set, and that consequently \(F\) is an inductive limit of ind \(p\)-groups, hence is an ind-\(p\)-group by 1.4 (ii). Conversely, suppose that for each \(\xi\) the stalk \(F_\xi\) is an ind-\(p\)-group, and let \(U \longrightarrow X\) be étale, \(U\) quasi-compact. Let \(S \subset F(U)\) be a finite subset. For each geometric point \(\xi\) of \(U\), the image of \(S\) in \(F_\xi\) generates a finite group. Since a finite group is of finite presentation, one concludes easily that there exists a \(U_\xi\) étale over \(U\), \(\xi\)-pointed, such that \(S\) generates a finite group in \(F(U_\xi)\) (cf. VIII 4). A finite number of such \(U_\xi\) form a covering of \(U\), say \(\{ U_1, \ldots, U_n \}\). Then the image of \(S\) in \(\prod F(U_i)\) generates a finite subgroup, and since \(F(U) \subset \prod F(U_i)\), we are done.
Assertion (ii) is trivial from (i), and (iii) is immediate.

footnotes.html: (∗) An object \(X\) of a topos is said to be quasi-compact if every covering family \(\{ X_i \longrightarrow X \}\) can be dominated by a finite covering family. A morphism \(u\) of topoi is quasi-compact if the inverse image of every quasi-compact object is again quasi-compact.

blocks.html: 2. Constructible sheaves

Let \(T\) be a topos. Recall that to each element \(S \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathrm{Ens})\) one associates the sheaf \(S_T\) associated to the presheaf \(P\) such that \(P(X) = S\) for each \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(T)\). The object of \(T\) that represents \(S_T\) is \[ \coprod_{s \in S} e = \text{"} S \times e \text{"} , \] \(e\) the final object of \(T\). \(S_T\) is called the constant sheaf, of value \(S\) (IV). One defines in an evident manner the notion of constant sheaf of groups, of constant \(A\)-modules (\(A\) a ring), and of constant abelian sheaf, of value \(M\). A morphism \(f_T : S_T \longrightarrow S'_T\) of constant sheaves is said to be constant if it comes from a morphism of sets \(f : S \longrightarrow S'\).
A sheaf \(F\) is said to be locally constant if there exists a covering \(\{ e_i \longrightarrow e \}\) of the final object such that \(F\) becomes constant on each \(e_i\).

One defines in an analogous way the notion of locally constant sheaf of groups or of \(A\)-modules, and of locally constant morphism \(f : F \to G\) if \(F\) and \(G\) are locally constant sheaves. Finally, a locally constant sheaf of groups or of \(A\)-modules is said to be of finite type (resp. of finite presentation) if the local values are groups or \(A\)-modules of finite type (resp. of finite presentation).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1

(i) Let \(f : F \to G\) be a morphism of locally constant sheaves of sets on \(T\), and suppose that the local values of \(F\) are finite sets. Then \(f\) is locally constant.

(ii) Let \(f : F \longrightarrow G\) be a morphism of locally constant sheaves of \(A\)-modules, with \(F\) of finite type. Then \(f\) is locally constant, and the kernel and cokernel of \(f\) are locally constant.

(iii) Let \(0 \to F' \to F \to F'' \to 0\) be an exact sequence of sheaves of \(A\)-modules (resp. of groups), with \(F'\) and \(F''\) locally constant, \(F''\) being of finite presentation. Then \(F\) is locally constant.

Proof of (i) and (ii). One reduces without difficulty to the case where \(F\) and \(G\) are constant. Let us treat (ii): let \(F = M_T\), \(G = N_T\) (\(M, N\) \(A\)-modules), and let \(S \subset M\) be a finite subset of generators of \(M\). Then \(f\) is determined by its restriction to \(S_T\) and \(f\) will be locally constant if \(f | S_T\) is. One is thus reduced to (i) for the first assertion of (ii), and the second assertion is a trivial consequence of the first.

It remains therefore to prove (i). Suppose that \(F = S_T\), \(G = S'_T\) are constant, and denote also by \(f\) the morphism of objects \(f : S \times e \longrightarrow S' \times e\) (notation as above). Let \(f_s : e \longrightarrow S' \times e\) (\(s \in S\)) be the components of \(f\): since \(S\) is finite, it evidently suffices to treat the case \(f = f_s\), that is, where \(S\) is a one-element set. Let \(X_{s'} \longrightarrow e\) (\(s' \in S'\)) be the family of morphisms making the diagrams \[ \xymatrix{ X_{s'} \ar[r] \ar[d] & e \ar[d]^{i_{s'}} \\ e \ar[r]_-{f} & S' \times e } \] cartesian, where \(i_{s'} : e \longrightarrow S' \times e\) is "the inclusion" into the \(s'\)-th component. The family \(\{ i_{s'} \}\) is trivially covering, so \(\{ X_{s'} \longrightarrow e \}\) is as well. One verifies immediately (since direct sums in a topos are disjoint) that \(f\) becomes constant on \(X_{s'}\), and that consequently \(f\) is locally constant.

Proof of (iii). Let us treat the case of sheaves of \(A\)-modules. One may suppose \(F'\) and \(F''\) constant, \(F''\) of value \(M''\) an \(A\)-module of finite presentation. If \(M''\) is free, hence admits a finite basis \((e_i)_{1 \leqslant i \leqslant n}\), then the \(e_i\) define sections of \(F''\), hence lift locally to sections of \(F\), which shows that locally the extension \(F\) of \(F''\) by \(F'\) splits, which proves that \(F\) is locally isomorphic to \(F' \times F''\), hence is locally constant. In the general case, choosing a surjective homomorphism \(\varphi : L'' \to M''\), with \(L''\) free of finite type; the kernel \(R\) of \(\varphi\) is of finite type, and setting \(L = L''_T \times_{M''_T} F\), \(F \simeq L''_T \times_{F''} F\); one sees on the one hand that \(L\) is an extension of \(L''_T\) by \(G\), hence locally constant by what precedes, and on the other hand that one has an exact sequence \(0 \longrightarrow R_T \longrightarrow L \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow 0\), which by (ii) implies that \(F\) is locally constant.
From now on, we restrict ourselves to the étale topoi of schemes.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.2

Let \(X\) be a scheme and \(F\) a sheaf on \(X\) that is locally constant. Then \(F\) is represented by a \(Y/X\) étale. If moreover the stalks of \(F\) are finite (resp. and non-empty), then \(Y\) is an étale covering (resp. and surjective).
Proof. Descent (SGA 1 IX 4.1 if \(F\) has finite stalks, SGA 3 X 5.4 in the general case).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.3

A sheaf of sets (resp. of groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules) is said to be constructible if for each affine open \(U \subset X\) there exists a decomposition of \(U\) into a union of a finite number of constructible locally closed reduced subschemes \(U_i\) such that the sheaf induced by \(F\) on each \(U_i\) is locally constant, of finite value (resp. finite, resp. of finite presentation(∗)).

The finiteness hypothesis on the local values amounts to saying that for each geometric point \(\xi\), the stalk \(F_\xi\) is finite (resp. finite, resp. of finite presentation). It follows immediately from 2.1 (i) that a sheaf of groups \(F\) is constructible if and only if the underlying sheaf of sets of \(F\) is constructible.

One should note that if \(F\) is an abelian sheaf, it is constructible as a sheaf of groups (or again, as a sheaf of sets) if and only if it is constructible as a sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}\)-modules, and if moreover its stalks are finite. Thus, \(\mathbb{Z}_X\) is constructible as a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module, but not as a sheaf of groups.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.4

(i) Let \(X\) be quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Then a sheaf (resp. sheaf of groups, resp. sheaf of \(A\)-modules) is construc- tible if and only if there exists a decomposition of \(X\) into a union of constructible locally closed parts, such that \(F\) becomes locally constant, and finite (resp. finite, resp. of finite presentation), on each \(X_i\).

(ii) To verify that \(F\) is constructible, it suffices to verify that \(F | U_i\) is constructible for the \(U_i\) of a given open covering of \(X\).

(iii) Let \(f : Y \longrightarrow X\) be a morphism. Then \(f^* F\) is constructible if \(F\) is.

(iv) The set of points where the stalk of a constructible sheaf is non- empty (resp. non-zero) is a locally constructible subset (EGA \(\mathrm{O_{III}}\) 9.1.2).

(v) Let \(X\) be locally noetherian. Then a sheaf of sets (resp. ...) \(F\) on \(X\) is constructible if and only if for each \(x \in X\), there exists a non-empty open of the closure \(\bar{x}\) of \(x\) such that \(F\) induces a locally constant sheaf of finite value (resp. ...) on \(U\).

Proof. Evidently, if \(f : Y \longrightarrow X\) is a morphism and if there exists a decomposition of \(X\) into a union of locally closed and constructible parts \(X_i\), such that \(F\) becomes locally constant on each \(X_i\), the same holds for \(Y\) and \(f^* F\) (cf. EGA IV 1.8.2). This proves the implication \(\Longleftarrow\) of (i). Suppose now that \(X\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated and let \(\{ U_1, \ldots, U_n \}\) be an affine open covering of \(X\) such that \(F | U_i\) is construc- tible for each \(i\). To find a decomposition of \(X\) as in (i), it suffices to do so for \(U_n\) and for \(Y = X - U_n\) (with the induced reduced structure), \(U_n\) and \(Y\) being constructible in \(X\) thanks to the hypothesis "\(X\) quasi- separated". Now a decomposition exists for \(U_n\) by the definition of construc- tibility, and \(Y\) is a union of \(n-1\) affine opens \(V_i = Y \cap U_i\) (\(i = 1, \ldots, n-1\)) with \(F | V_i\) constructible, whence the result (i) by induction on \(n\). The same reasoning proves (ii); indeed, the hypothesis implies that \(F | U\) is constructible for each "sufficiently small" affine open \(U\), and one can cover an arbitrary affine open \(V\) by a finite number of such opens. Assertion (ii) shows that the notion of constructibility is local on \(X\), and (iii), (iv) follow immediately. The implication \(\Longrightarrow\) of (v) is immediate, and does not depend on the noetherian hypothesis. If \(X\) is noetherian one proves the implication \(\Longleftarrow\) by the usual "noetherian induction".

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.5

Let \(X\) be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and \(F\) a constructible sheaf of groups or of \(A\)-modules on \(X\). Then there exists a filtra- tion of \(F\) whose successive quotients are of the form \(i_! G\), where \(i : U \to X\) is the inclusion of a locally closed and constructible part, and where \(G\) is locally constant and constructible on \(U\). If \(X\) is noetherian, there exists such a filtration, with the \(U\) irreducible.

Proof. By 2.4 (i), there exists a decomposition of \(X\) into a finite union of constructible locally closed parts \(X_i\) such that each \(F | X_i\) is locally constant and finite (resp. of finite presentation). Let us write \(X_i = U_i \cap \complement V_i\), where \(U_i\) and \(V_i\) are constructible opens, and let \(N\) be the number of opens of \(X\) in the sub-topology \(T\) generated by \(\{ U_i, V_i \}\). Let us argue by induction on \(N\): if \(W\) is a minimal non-empty element of \(T\), it is evident that \(F | W\) is locally constant and of finite presentation. Let \(i : W \to X\) be the inclusion morphism and \(Y = X - W\). One has the exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow i_! i^* F \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow F | Y \longrightarrow 0 , \] and one thus reduces to the same assertion for \(Y\) and for the sheaf \(F | Y\), where one can apply the induction hypothesis.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6

Suppose that \(A\) is a noetherian ring.

(i) A finite projective (resp. inductive) limit of constructible sheaves of \(A\)-modules or of sets is constructible. In particular, the kernel, the cokernel and the image of a morphism of constructible sheaves of \(A\)-modules are constructible.

(ibis) A finite projective limit of constructible sheaves of sets (resp. of groups) is constructible, and if \(f : F \longrightarrow G\) is a morphism of constructible sheaves of groups, the kernel, the image, and the cokernel (if \(\operatorname{Im}(f)\) is a normal subgroup) are constructible. A finite inductive limit of constructible sheaves of sets is constructible.

(ii) Let \(0 \longrightarrow M' \longrightarrow M \longrightarrow M'' \longrightarrow 0\) be an exact sequence of sheaves of \(A\)-modules (resp. of groups) with \(M'\), \(M''\) constructible. Then \(M\) is constructible.

(iii) Let \(M_1 \longrightarrow M_2 \longrightarrow M_3 \longrightarrow M_4 \longrightarrow M_5\) be an exact sequence of sheaves of \(A\)-modules. Then if \(M_i\) is constructible for \(i = 1,2,4,5\), the same holds for \(i = 3\).

Proof. (i) We leave the set-theoretic and group assertions to the reader. For the case of sheaves of \(A\)-modules, it suffices to prove that the kernel and the cokernel of a morphism \(f : F \to G\) of constructible sheaves of \(A\)-modules are constructible. The assertion is local on \(X\), and one may therefore suppose \(X\) affine, hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Then one reduces to the case where \(F\) and \(G\) are locally constant by 2.4 (i), and one concludes using 2.1 (ii) and the noetherian hypothesis on \(A\). One proves assertion (ii) in an analogous way using 2.1 (iii). Assertion (iii) is immediate from (i) and (ii).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.7

Let \(X\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme, \(F\) a sheaf of sets (resp. of \(A\)-modules). For \(F\) to be constructible, it is necessary and sufficient that it be isomorphic to the cokernel of a pair of morphisms \(H \rightrightarrows G\), where \(H\) and \(G\) are sheaves of sets representable by étale schemes of finite presentation over \(X\) (resp. that \(F\) be isomorphic to the cokernel of a homomorphism \(A_{V,X} \longrightarrow A_{U,X}\), where \(U\) and \(V\) are two schemes étale of finite presentation over \(X\)).
The sufficiency follows easily from 2.6 (ibis).

Suppose that \(F\) is a constructible sheaf of sets. Using the existence of infinite sums in the étale site over \(X\), one sees that one can find an epimorphism \(G \to F\), with \(G\) representable by an étale scheme over \(X\), which one may moreover suppose to be a sum of affine schemes \(G_i\) (\(i \in I\)), hence separated over \(S\). For every finite part \(J\) of the index set \(I\), let \(G_J\) be the sum of the \(G_i\) for \(i \in J\), \(F_J\) its image in \(F\). Since \(G_J\) and \(F\) are constructible, so is \(F_J\) (2.6 (ibis)), hence the set \(X_J\) of \(x \in X\) such that the stalks of \(F\) and \(F_J\) at a geometric point of \(X\) over \(x\) are equal, is locally constructible 2.4 (iv). Since the family of the \(X_J\) is increasing and has union \(X\), and since \(X\) is quasi-compact, one of the \(X_J\) is equal to \(X\) (EGA IV 1.9.9). This shows, after replacing \(G\) by \(G_J\), that one may suppose \(G\) affine, hence separated over \(S\), and quasi-compact over \(X\) since \(X\) is quasi-separated (EGA IV 1.2.4). Let then \(H = G \times_X G\). It is a subsheaf of \(G \times_S G\) which is representable, hence is itself representable (VIII 6.1). Since \(G\) is moreover constructible (2.6 (ibis)), it follows again from the preceding argument that it is quasi-compact, hence (being separated over \(X\)) of finite presentation over \(X\). This proves the first assertion of 2.7, and the second is proved by the same method (NB it is not necessary that \(A\) be noetherian). Let us point out in passing that the proof also proves the following corollary:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.7.1

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(F\) a scheme étale over \(X\). For the corresponding étale sheaf on \(X\) to be constructible, it is necessary and sufficient that \(F\) be of finite presentation over \(X\).
Proposition 2.7 will be useful to us above all here for deriving certain properties of passage to the limit for constructible sheaves:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.7.2

Let \(X\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme. Then every sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(p\)-groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules) on \(X\) is an inductive limit of a filtered inductive system of constructible sheaves of sets (resp. ...).

If \(F\) is a sheaf of sets, let us resume the notation of the proof of 2.7, and let \(L\) be the set of pairs \((J, H')\), where \(J\) is a finite part of \(I\) and \(H'\) a quasi-compact open part of \(H_J = G_J \times_F G_J\). We order \(L\) in the obvious way, and one observes that, since \(F\) is the limit of the \(F_J\), and each \(F_J\) is the limit of \(\operatorname{Coker}(H' \rightrightarrows G_J)\) for the quasi-compact opens \(H'\) of \(H_J\), that \(F\) is the inductive limit of the inductive system of the \(F_\ell = \operatorname{Coker}(H' \rightrightarrows F_J)\) for \(\ell = (H', J) \in L\), whence the set-theoretic case. The case of sheaves of \(A\)-modules is treated in essentially the same way, by beginning with representing \(F\) as the cokernel of a homomorphism \(A_{V,X} \longrightarrow A_{U,X}\), with \(U, V\) schemes étale and separated over \(X\). The case of ind-\(p\)-groups demands a little more attention. Resuming the preceding notation, we denote by \(L(G_J)\) the free sheaf of groups generated by the sheaf of sets \(G_J\), by \(N_J\) the kernel of the homomorphism \(L(G_J) \to F\) deduced from \(G_J \to F\), by \(L\) the set of pairs \((J, N')\), where \(N'\) is a subsheaf of sets of \(N_J\) that is "quasi-compact", i.e. such that there exists an epimorphism \(P \to N'\), with \(P\) representable by a quasi-compact \(X\)-scheme. We order \(L\) by declaring that \((J, N')\) is smaller than \((J_1, N'_1)\) if \(J \subset J_1\) and if the canonical homomorphism \(L(G_J) \to L(G_{J_1})\) maps \(N'\) into \(N'_1\). It is immediate that \(L\) is filtered, and that one obtains an inductive system of sheaves of groups \(F_\ell\), indexed by \(L\), by taking, for \(\ell = (J, N')\), \(F_\ell = \) the quotient sheaf of groups of \(L(G_J)\) by the invariant subsheaf of groups generated by \(N'\). It is moreover immediate that \(F\) is isomorphic to the inductive limit of the \(F_\ell\), and it remains to prove that there exists a part \(L'\) of \(L\), cofinal in \(L\), such that for \(\ell \in L'\), \(F_\ell\) is a constructible sheaf of \(p\)-groups. For this, it suffices to prove that for every \(J\), one can find a sub- sheaf of sets \(N'\) of \(N_J\) that is quasi-compact, contains a given quasi-compact subsheaf of sets \(N'_0\), and is such that the corresponding \(F_\ell\) is a constructible sheaf of \(p\)-groups. Let us first note that it suffices, for this, that the stalks of \(F_\ell\) be finite \(p\)-groups: then \(F_\ell\) will automatically be constructible, as the reader will verify without difficulty. On the other hand, the reader may also verify that the set \(X_{N'}\) of points \(x\) of \(X\) such that the stalk of \(F_\ell\) at a geometric point above \(x\) is a finite \(p\)-group is locally constructible. Moreover, the parts \(X_{N'}\) of \(X\) are an increasing function of \(N'\), and finally their union is all of \(X\): this last point results from the fact that the inductive limit of the \(F_\ell\), for \(\ell = (N', J)\) with \(J\) fixed, is the subsheaf of groups \(F_J\) of \(F\) generated by the subsheaf of sets \(G_J\), and \(F_J\) has finite \(p\)-groups as stalks. On the other hand, in a free group with a finite number of generators, every subgroup of finite index is a free subgroup with a finite number of generators, hence if it is represented as a filtered union of its finite parts, one of these generates the whole subgroup. From this it follows easily that the union of the \(X_{N'}\) is indeed \(X\). Using again (EGA IV 1.9.9) one finds that one of the \(X_{N'}\) is equal to \(X\), which completes the proof of 2.7.2.

Let us note that the somewhat painful proof of the case of sheaves of groups brings to light the lack of a convenient sorites for the constructibility conditions for sheaves of groups whose stalks are not necessarily finite; we apologize to the reader for this, inviting him if need be to fill this gap by his own means, and we point out to him by way of consolation that in 2.9 (iii) we obtain a simpler proof when \(X\) is noetherian.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.7.3

Let \(X\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme, \(F\) a constructible sheaf of sets (resp. of \(A\)-modules). Then the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}(F,G)\), where \(G\) is a variable sheaf of sets (resp. ...), commutes with inductive limits in \(G\). In the case where \(F\) is a sheaf of \(A\)-modules, \(A\) being noetherian, the functors \(\operatorname{Ext}^i(X; F, G)\) in the \(A\)-module \(G\) likewise commute with inductive limits.
This follows from 2.7 and (VII 3.3) by the usual arguments, which are left to the reader. Similarly, the conjunction of 2.7 and the results of (VII 5) easily gives:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.7.4

Let \(I\) be a filtered category, \(i \mapsto X_i : I^{\circ} \to (\mathrm{Sch})\) a functor that transforms arrows into affine morphisms and objects into quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes. For every scheme \(Y\), let \(F_c(Y)\) be the category of constructible sheaves of sets (resp. of ind-\(p\)-groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules) on \(Y\). Then one has an equivalence of categories \[ F_c(X) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_i F_c(X_i) , \] where \(X = \varprojlim_i X_i\) (VII 5) and where the second member denotes the category \(\varprojlim\) of fibred categories, defined in . In particular, every constructible sheaf of sets (resp. ...) on \(X\) is isomorphic to the inverse image of a sheaf of the same nature on one of the \(X_i\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.8

Let \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a surjective morphism, locally of finite presentation, and let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. ...) on \(Y\). Then \(F\) is constructible if and only if \(f^*(F)\) is.
We shall use the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.8.1

Let \(f : X \longrightarrow Y\) be a surjective morphism, locally of finite presenta- tion, with \(Y\) quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Then there exists a finite partition of \(Y\) into subschemes \(Y_i\) of finite presentation over \(Y\) (in particular each \(Y_i\) is constructible in \(X\)) and, for every \(i\), morphisms finite surjective \(Y''_i \xrightarrow{\ g_i\ } Y'_i \xrightarrow{\ h_i\ } Y_i\), with \(h_i\) étale and \(g_i\) locally free (i.e. flat and of finite presentation, in addition to the condition \(g_i\) finite), and radicial, and finally a \(Y\)-morphism \(Y''_i \longrightarrow X\)(∗).

Using the fact that \(Y\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, one reduces easily to the case where \(Y\) is quasi-affine hence separated (by using an affine open finite covering \((U_i)_{1 \leqslant i \leqslant n}\) of \(Y\) and considering the \(Y_i = U_i - U_i \cap \bigcup_{j < i} U_j\), then to the case \(Y\) affine (by the same argument). The scheme \(X\) is a union of affine opens \(X_i\), and the image \(T_i\) of \(X_i\) in \(Y\) is constructible (EGA IV 1.8.4), the union of the \(T_i\) is \(Y\) since \(f\) is surjective, whence it follows that \(X\) is a union of a finite number of the \(T_i\) (EGA IV 1.9.9), so that, re- placing \(X\) by the sum scheme of the corresponding \(X_i\), one may suppose \(X\) affine. Then the standard passage-to-the-limit procedure (EGA IV 8 8.1.2 c)) allows us to suppose moreover that \(Y\) is noetherian. The usual noetherian induction, and the passage-to-the-limit procedure (EGA IV 8.1.2 a)) reduce us to the case where \(Y\) is reduced to the spectrum of a field \(k\). Since then \(X \neq \emptyset\), there exists a closed point \(x \in X\), which corresponds to a finite extension \(k'\) of \(k\), itself a radicial extension of a separable extension \(k'_s\) of \(k\). One then takes \(Y' = \operatorname{Spec}(k'_s)\), \(Y'' = \operatorname{Spec}(k')\), which completes the proof of 2.8.1.

The necessity in 2.8 being trivial (2.4 (iii)), let us prove the suffi- ciency. One is then reduced, by the preceding lemma, to the case where \(f\) is of the form \(g h\), where \(g\) and \(h\) satisfy the conditions stated for \(g_i, h_i\) in the lemma. One may therefore suppose successively either that \(f\) is finite radicial, a trivial case by (VIII 1.1), or that \(f\) is finite étale. Let us note moreover that, using the hypothesis that \(f^*(F)\) is constructible and the definition of constructibility, we could suppose (after replacing \(X\) by an \(X\)-prescheme \(X' \simeq \coprod_i X_i\) of finite presentation and with surjective structural morphism) that \(f^*(F)\) is already locally constant. But when \(f\) is étale and surjective, this implies that \(F\) is locally constant. Since moreover all the hypotheses made on the stalks of \(f^*(F)\) remain valid for those of \(F\), \(f\) being surjective, it indeed follows that \(F\) is constructible, which completes the proof of 2.8.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.9

Let \(X\) be a noetherian scheme, \(A\) a noetherian ring, and \(p\) a set of prime numbers.

(i) The category of sheaves of sets (resp. of ind \(p\)-groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules) on \(X\) is locally noetherian, that is, possesses a set of generators formed of noetherian objects.

(ii) A sheaf \(F\) of sets (resp. of ind \(p\)-groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules) on \(X\) is constructible if and only if it is noetherian. If \(F\) is a sheaf of \(A\)-modules, then \(F\) is constructible if and only if it is a quotient of a finite sum of sheaves of the form \(A_{U/X}\), where \(U \longrightarrow X\) is étale and of finite type (notation of IV.2.4: \(A_{U/X} = A_U\)).

(iii) The constructible subsheaves of a sheaf \(F\) of sets (resp. ...) form an inductive system, and \(F\) is the inductive limit of these subsheaves.

Proof. We leave the set-theoretic assertion to the reader. Let us treat first the case of a sheaf of \(A\)-modules. For (i) one must find a set of generators whose elements are noetherian objects. Now the sheaves of the form \(A_{U/X}\), \(U \longrightarrow X\) étale and of finite type, form a set of genera- tors which one sees easily to be constructible, and it therefore suffices to prove the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.10

Let \(X\) be noetherian. Then every constructible \(A\)-Module is noetherian.
Proof of the lemma.

By noetherian induction we suppose the lemma true for each subscheme \(X'\) of \(X\) distinct from \(X\). Let us take a non-empty open \(X_0\) of \(X\) such that \(F\) induces a locally constant sheaf \(F_0\) on \(X_0\).

Let now \(\{ F_i \}\), \(i \in \mathbb{N}\) be an increasing sequence of subsheaves of \(F_0\). Since for a geometric point \(P\), generic for an irreducible component of \(X_0\), the stalk of \(F_0\) at \(P\) is of finite type, the sequence of stalks \((F_i)_P\) is stationary, and we may suppose it constant. Now let \(Q\) be a geometric point of \(X_0\) that is a specialization of \(P\) (VIII 7.2). Since \(F_0\) is locally constant on \(X_0\), one sees immediately that the specialization morphism \(F_{0_Q} \longrightarrow F_{0_P}\) (VIII.7) is bijective, so \((F_i)_Q \longrightarrow (F_i)_P\) is injective for each \(i\).

Let \(V/X\) be étale and \(P\)-pointed, and \(s_1, \ldots, s_n\) sections \(\in F_1(V)\) that generate \((F_i)_P\). Then the \(s_i\) generate \((F_i)_Q\) for each \(i\) and each geometric point \(Q\) that is a specialization of \(P\) above \(V\). The sequence of sheaves \(F_i\) is therefore constant in a neighbourhood of the image of \(P\), say in \(X' \neq \emptyset\). Let \(Y = X - X'\); it therefore suffices to prove that the sequence of the \(F_i | Y\) is stationary, which follows from the noetherian induction hypothesis.

Assertions (ii) for the \(A\)-modules are now immediate: Since the \(A_{U/X}\) are noetherian generators, one evidently has \(F\) noetherian \(\Longleftrightarrow F\) is a quotient of a finite sum of sheaves \(A_{U/X}\). Now \(A_{U/X}\) is constructible, and consequently, taking 2.6 into account, \(F\) noetherian \(\Longrightarrow F\) constructible; the reverse implication being already established (2.10), this establishes (ii). Finally, assertion (iii) for the \(A\)-modules is a property of locally noetherian categories (cf. [1], Ch. IV).

Let us now treat the case of ind-\(p\)-groups. Let us first note that a constructible sheaf of groups \(F\) is certainly noetherian. Indeed, since the stalks are finite, one can employ the same argument as with the \(A\)-modules. We shall now prove assertion (iii) directly, which will imply (i) — indeed, this will show that the constructible sheaves form a set of generators. Moreover, an arbitrary noetherian sheaf will then necessarily be constructible, whence (ii).

To prove (iii), it evidently suffices to prove that a sub- sheaf (of groups) \(S\) of a sheaf \(F\) of ind \(p\)-groups generated by a finite number of sections \(s_i \in F(U_i)\), \(U_i \longrightarrow X\) étale of finite type, is constructible(∗).

(Since a constructible sheaf is noetherian, it is generated by a finite number of sections.) By noetherian induction, one may suppose that this is true for each closed subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\), distinct from \(X\). Now the notion of sub- sheaf generated by sections commutes with the inverse image of sheaves; in effect, let \(L_{U/X}\) be the sheaf that represents the functor \(F \longmapsto F(U)\) in the category of groups. Then if \(f : Y \longrightarrow X\), one has \(f^*(L_{U/X}) = L_{U \times_X Y/Y}\). Since \(S\) is the image of the sum of the \(L_{U_i/X}\), and since \(f^*\) commutes with sums, it is clear that \(f^* S\) is the subsheaf of \(f^* F\) generated by the sections \(f^*(S_i)\).

One may therefore suppose that \(S\) induces a constructible sheaf on each closed \(Y\) distinct from \(X\), and it thus suffices (2.4 (i)) to prove that \(S\) induces a constructible sheaf on a suitable non-empty open of \(X\). By replacing \(X\) by a sufficiently small open, one may suppose that each \(U_i\) is an étale covering of \(X\). It suffices to prove that then \(S\) is locally constant, with finite stalks on a suitable non-empty open. This is a local assertion on \(X\) for the étale topology, and one may therefore suppose each \(U_i\) is completely decomposed, say \(U_i = \coprod_{n_i} X\) (sum of \(n_i\) copies of \(X\)). Let \(s_{ij}\) (\(j = 1, \ldots, n_i\)) be the sections of \(F(X)\) such that \(s_i\) \((s_{i1}, \ldots, s_{in_i})\). Evidently, \(S\) is none other than the subsheaf of \(F\) generated by the \(s_{ij} \in F(X)\). Since \(F(X)\) is an ind \(p\)-group (1.5) the \(s_{ij}\) generate a finite subgroup 1.3. So one may suppose that the set of the \(s_i\) is a finite sub- group of \(F(X)\), but then \(S\) is identical to the sheaf of sets generated by the \(s_i\), which is constructible by virtue of 2.6 (i) as a sheaf of sets, hence as a sheaf of groups, q.e.d.
In the two following propositions, we give criteria for a sheaf to be locally constant, or constructible, using the specialization homomorphisms (VIII 7.7).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.11

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(F\) a constructible sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-finite groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules); in the set-theoretic case, one supposes moreover \(F\) has finite stalks. Let \(x \in X\), \(\bar{x}\) a geometric point over \(x\). For \(F\) to be locally constant in a neighbourhood of \(x\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every geometric point \(\bar{x}'\) generization of \(\bar{x}\), and every specialization arrow \(\bar{x}' \to \bar{x}\) (VIII 7.2), the specialization homomorphism (VIII 7.7) \(F_{\bar{x}} \to F_{\bar{x}'}\), be an isomorphism.

The case of a sheaf of groups being a special case of that of a sheaf of sets, we content ourselves with treating the latter; the case of a sheaf of modules is treated in essentially the same way. The necessity of the condition being trivial, we confine ourselves to establishing the sufficiency. Since the stalk \(I = F_{\bar{x}}\) is finite, after replacing \(X\) by a suitable scheme \(X'\) étale over \(X\), one may suppose that one can find a homomorphism \(u : I_X \longrightarrow F\) from the constant sheaf \(I_X\) to \(F\), inducing an isomorphism on the stalks at \(\bar{x}\). Using the constructibility of the two sheaves, and 2.6, one sees easily that the set \(Z\) of points \(z\) of \(X\) such that the homomorphism induced on the stalks at a geometric point \(\bar{z}\) over \(z\) is bijective, is a locally constructible part of \(X\). The hypothesis immediately implies that it contains the genera- tions of \(x\), hence (EGA IV 1.10.1) it is a neighbourhood of \(x\), which proves that \(F\) is locally constant (in this case, even constant) in a neighbourhood of \(x\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.12(∗)

A scheme \(X\) is said to be arcwise connected if for every pair \(P, Q\) of geometric points of \(X\), there exist geometric points \(P = P_0, \ldots, P_n\); \(Q_1, \ldots, Q_n = Q\) and specializations (VIII 7.2) \(P_i \longrightarrow Q_i\) and \(P_{i-1} \longrightarrow Q_i\) (\(i = 1, \ldots, n\)). One says that \(X\) is locally arcwise connected (for the étale topology) if for each \(U \longrightarrow X\) étale there exists an étale covering \(\{ U_i \longrightarrow U \}\) of \(U\) such that \(U_i\) is arcwise connected for each \(i\).
One verifies immediately that a locally noetherian prescheme is locally arcwise connected.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.13

(i) Let \(X\) be locally arcwise connected and let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. of groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules) on \(X\). Suppose that the stalks of \(F\) are finite (resp. finite, resp. of finite presentation). Then \(F\) is locally constant if and only if for every specialization \(P \longrightarrow Q\) of geometric points, the specialization morphism (VIII 7.7) \(F_Q \longrightarrow F_P\) is bijective.

(ii) Suppose that \(X\) is locally noetherian and that the stalks of \(F\) are finite (resp. finite, resp. of finite presentation). Then, if for every specialization \(P \longrightarrow Q\), the specialization morphism \(F_Q \longrightarrow F_P\) is injec- tive, \(F\) is constructible.

(iii) Suppose that \(X\) is locally noetherian and that the stalks of the sheaf of sets \(F\) are finite. Let \(c : X \longrightarrow \mathbb{N}\) be the function that to \(x \in X\) associates the number of elements of the stalk \(F_{\bar{x}}\) of \(F\) at a geome- tric point \(\bar{x}\) above \(x\). Then \(F\) is constructible if and only if \(c\) is a constructible function, i.e., if and only if \(c^{-1}(n)\) is construc- tible for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

Proof. (i) Let \(P\) be a geometric point of \(X\). We shall find an étale neighbourhood of \(P\), that is, a \(U \longrightarrow X\) étale \(P\)-pointed, such that \(F\) becomes constant on \(U\). Let \(V'\) be an étale neighbourhood of \(P\) such that \(F(V) \longrightarrow F_P\) is surjective. Such a \(V'\) exists by the finiteness hypothesis. Let \(U \longrightarrow V'\) be an étale neighbourhood of \(P\) in \(V'\), such that \(U\) is arcwise connected. Then \(F(U) \longrightarrow F_P\) is still surjective. Let us choose a subset \(S \subset F(U)\) that maps bijectively onto \(F_P\). If \(F\) is a sheaf of groups (resp. of \(A\)-modules), one sees easily that one can, by changing \(U\) if need be, find such a set that is moreover a subgroup (resp. submodule) of \(F(U)\). One deduces a morphism \(S_U \longrightarrow F | U\), where \(S_U\) is the constant sheaf of value \(S\). One has \[ (S_U)_P \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F_P . \]
Since each specialization morphism on the stalks of \(F\) (resp. \(S_U\)) is bijective, and since \(U\) is arcwise connected, it follows that \(S_U \xrightarrow{\sim} F | U\), whence the result.

(ii) The assertion is local, and one may therefore suppose \(X\) noetherian. Let \(P\) be a geometric point above a maximal point of \(X\). There exists an irreducible, hence arcwise connected, étale neighbourhood \(U \longrightarrow X\) of \(P\) such that \(F(U)\) maps surjectively onto \(F_P\). It then maps surjectively onto \(F_Q\) for each geometric point \(Q\) of \(V\), or what amounts to the same, for each geometric point of the image \(U\) of \(V\) in \(X\), for such a point is a specialization of \(P\) and \(F_Q \longrightarrow F_P\) is injective. So each specialization morphism in \(U\) is bijective, hence \(F | U\) is locally constant. By noetherian induction one may suppose that \(F | X - U\) is constructible, whence the result.

(iii) It clearly suffices to treat the case where the function \(c\) is constant. Let \(V \longrightarrow X\) be an étale neighbourhood of a geometric point \(P\) lying over a maximal point of \(X\), such that \(F(V)\) maps surjectively onto \(F_P\). Let \(S\) be a subset of \(F(V)\) such that \(S \xrightarrow{\sim} F_P\). Then, for the constant sheaf \(S_V\) and for each specialization \(P \longrightarrow Q\) of geometric points, we have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ (S_V)_P \ar[r]^-{\sim} & F_P \\ (S_V)_Q \ar[u] \ar[r] & F_Q \ar[u] } \] Since \(c(F_Q) = c(F_P)\), the arrow \(F_Q \longrightarrow F_P\) is bijective, hence \(F\) is locally constant in a neighbourhood of \(P\) by (i). By noetherian induction, we are done.
The following result (ii) will be of technical use in what follows; it will allow certain verifications to be reduced to the case of a constant sheaf.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.14

Let \(X\) be a scheme.

(i) For every finite morphism of finite presentation \(f : X' \to X\), and every sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-finite groups, resp. of \(A\)-modules) constructible on \(X'\), \(f_*(F)\) is constructible.

(ii) Suppose \(X\) quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. ...) constructible on \(X\). Then one can find a finite family \((p_i : X'_i \longrightarrow X)\) of finite morphisms, for each \(i\), a constructible constant sheaf of sets (resp. ...) \(C_i\) on \(X'_i\), and a monomorphism \[ F \hookrightarrow \prod_i p_{i*}(C_i) . \]

Let us first prove (i). By definition, we may assume \(X\) affine, and then, using 2.7.4, the standard passage to the limit reduces us to the case where \(X\) is noetherian. A further passage to the limit, again using 2.7.4, and moreover 2.4 (v), reduces us to the case where \(X\) is the spectrum of a field. Then the conclusion reduces to the corresponding assertion on the stalk of \(f_*(F)\) at a geometric point over \(X\), which follows immediately from (VIII 5.5, 5.8).

Let us prove (ii). By virtue of 2.4 (i), there exists a partition of \(X\) into subschemes \(Y_i\), with inclusion morphisms \(u_i : Y_i \longrightarrow X\) of finite presentation, such that the restriction \(F_i\) of \(F\) to each \(Y_i\) is a locally constant sheaf. It is then immediate that the canonical homomorphisms \(F \longrightarrow u_{i*}(F_i)\) define a homomorphism \(F \longrightarrow \prod_i u_{i*}(F_i)\) which is a monomorphism.

One could even arrange in the preceding construction for each \(F_i\) to be, not only locally constant, but moreover isotrivial, i.e. that there exists a surjective finite étale morphism \(q_i : Y'_i \longrightarrow Y_i\) such that \(q_i^*(F_i)\) is a constant sheaf on \(Y'_i\), say \(C_{i\,Y'_i}\). This follows easily, for example, from the definition of 2.8.1 and from (VIII 1.1). On the other hand, it follows from the "Main Theorem" in the form (EGA IV 8.12.6) that there exist a finite morphism \(p_i : Z_i \longrightarrow X\) and an open immersion \(v_i : Y'_i \longrightarrow Z_i\) of \(X\)-schemes.

Since \(F_i\) embeds into \(q_{i*}(q_i^*(F_i)) = q_{i*}(C_{i\,Y'_i})\), \(F\) embeds into the product of the \(u_{i*}(q_{i*}(C_{i\,Y'_i})) = p_{i*}(v_{i*}(C_{i\,Y'_i}))\). If every \(Z_i\) is normal, then the lemma \((2.14.1)\) below implies that \(v_{i*}(C_{i\,Y'_i}) \xrightarrow{\sim} C_{i\,Z_i}\), hence \(F\) embeds into the product of the \(p_{i*}(C_{i\,Z_i})\), and we are done. In the general case, let us introduce the normalization \(\overline{Z}_i\) of \(Z_i\), the inverse image \(\overline{Y}'_i\) of \(Y'_i\) in \(\overline{Z}_i\), and the immersion \(\overline{v}_i : \overline{Y}'_i \longrightarrow \overline{Z}_i\). One sees at once that \(\overline{Y}'_i\) contains the maximal points of \(\overline{Z}_i\), hence is dense in \(\overline{Z}_i\). If \(r_i : \overline{Z}_i \to Z_i\) and \(s_i : \overline{Y}'_i \to Y'_i\) are the projections, then, since the latter is surjective, it follows that \(C_{i\,Y'_i}\) embeds into \(s_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Y}'_i})\), hence \(v_{i*}(C_{i\,Y'_i})\) embeds into \(v_{i*}(s_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Y}'_i})) = r_{i*}(\overline{v}_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Y}'_i}))\), which is isomorphic to \(r_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Z}_i})\) by virtue of \((2.14.1)\) below. Hence \(F\) embeds into the product of the \(p_{i*}(r_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Z}_i})) = t_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Z}_i})\), where \(t_i = p_i r_i\) is the canonical projection \(\overline{Z}_i \to X\). When this morphism is finite for every \(i\), we are therefore done. In the general case, we can only say that \(\overline{Z}_i\) is integral over \(X\), hence of the form \(\operatorname{Spec}(A_i)\), where \(A_i\) is a quasi-coherent sheaf of \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-Algebras which is integral over \(\mathcal{O}_X\). Using (EGA IV 1.7.7), one sees that \(A_i\) is the inductive limit of its sub-Algebras \(A_{i,j}\) finite over \(X\), hence \(\overline{Z}_i\) is the projective limit (VII 5) of the preschemes \(Z_{i\,j} = \operatorname{Spec}(A_{ij})\), finite over \(X\). Applying (VII 5.11), we find that \(t_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Z}_i})\) is the inductive limit of the \(t_{ij*}(C_{i\,Z_{ij}})\) where \(t_{ij} : Z_{ij} \to X\) is the canonical projection. By virtue of (2.7.3), the homomorphism \(F \longrightarrow t_{i*}(C_{i\,\overline{Z}_i})\) therefore factors through a homomorphism \(F \longrightarrow t_{ij*}(C_{i\,Z_{ij}})\), for a suitable \(j = j(i)\). We now set \(X'_i = Z_{i,j(i)}\), and we obtain an embedding as announced in 2.14.
It remains to prove the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.14.1

Let \(X\) be a geometrically unibranch scheme (for example normal), \(i : U \longrightarrow X\) a quasi-compact open immersion. Then the closure \(Z\) of \(U\), equipped with the induced reduced structure, is likewise geometrically unibranch; more precisely, for every \(z \in Z\), one has \(\mathcal{O}_{Z,z} \xleftarrow{\sim} \mathcal{O}_{X_{\text{red}},z}\). Suppose on the other hand that \(i\) is dominant, and let \(C\) be a set, \(C_U\) the constant sheaf on \(U\) defined by \(C\). Then the natural homomorphism \(C_U \longrightarrow i_*(C_U)\) is an isomorphism. The same conclusions hold if one replaces the open immersion \(i\) by an inclusion \(i : x \to X\), where \(x\) is a maximal point of \(X\).

Using (EGA IV 2.3.11), we are reduced, for the first assertion, to the case where \(X\) is local, with closed point \(z\), but then \(X_{\text{red}}\) is integral and \(U\) nonempty, hence \(Z = X_{\text{red}}\) and the assertion is obvious (it would therefore have sufficed, instead of \(X\) geometrically unibranch, to assume here that the local rings of \(X_{\text{red}}\) are integral). For the second assertion, arguing fibre by fibre, we reduce, thanks to (VIII 5.3) and loc. cit., to the case where \(X\) is strictly local, and to proving then that \(H^0(X, C_X) \longrightarrow H^0(U, C_U)\) is bijective. But here again, \(X\) is irreducible, and \(U\) is a nonempty open of it, hence irreducible, and the two sides of the preceding map are both identified with \(C\), whence the desired conclusion. (We have here used the notion "geometrically unibranch" in the form of (EGA IV 18.8.14), as meaning that the strict localized rings of \(X_{\text{red}}\) are integral. The case of the inclusion of a maximal point (stated here for the convenience of future references) is treated in exactly the same way.

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 2.14.2

When \(X\) is noetherian, the proof given (or an immediate deduction from it) shows that in 2.14 (ii), one may assume the \(X'_i\) integral; if moreover one assumes \(X\) universally Japanese, i.e. the rings of its affine opens universally Japanese (EGA \(\mathrm{O_{IV}}\) 23.1.1, IV 7.7.2), one may moreover assume the \(X'_i\) normal.

footnotes.html: (∗) When \(A\) is not assumed noetherian, it is preferable, for the needs of Homological Algebra, to require here, instead of merely finite presentation for the \(A\)-module \(M\), that it admit a left resolution by free \(A\)-modules of finite type. The notion introduced in (2.3) should then take the name: \(F\) is 1-constructible, (more generally, one would define in an obvious way \(n\)-constructibility, for every integer \(n \geqslant 0\)). For the present exposé we shall provisionally keep the terminology in the form (2.3), which is reasonable above all in the case where \(A\) is noetherian, where it coincides with the one just mentioned. Compare SGA 6 I for notions of finiteness in non-noetherian cases.
(∗) This statement is also given in EGA IV 17.16.4.

(∗) Let us recall the definition of this sheaf: let \(L_{U/X}\) be the sheaf that represents the functor \(F \mapsto F(U)\) in the category of groups. The section \(s_i \in F(U_i)\) induces a morphism \(L_{U_i/X} \to F\), and \(S\) is the image of the sum morphism \(\coprod_i L_{U_i/X} \to F\). It is the smallest subsheaf that "contains" the sections \(s_i\).
(∗) The terminology is due to S. Lubkin.

blocks.html: 3. Kummer and Artin-Schreier theories

We shall denote by \((\mathbb{G}_m)_X\) the sheaf represented by the multiplicative group \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_X[t, t^{-1}]\) over \(X\). Thus for \(U \longrightarrow X\) étale, the sections of \((\mathbb{G}_m)_X\) over \(U\) are the invertible elements \(\Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}^*_U)\) of \(\Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}_U)\). Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). The kernel of the \(n\)-th power in \((\mathbb{G}_m)_X\) is the "sheaf of \(n\)-th roots of unity", denoted \((\mu_n)_X\). We thus have an exact sequence \[ (3.1) \qquad 0 \longrightarrow (\mu_n)_X \longrightarrow (\mathbb{G}_m)_X \xrightarrow{\ n\ } (\mathbb{G}_m)_X . \]
If \(n\) is invertible on \(X\) (that is, if \(n\) is prime to each residue characteristic of \(X\)), the \(n\)-th power is a surjective morphism for sheaves:

blocks.title: Kummer Theory
blocks.html:
Kummer Theory 3.2

We have the exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow (\mu_n)_X \longrightarrow (\mathbb{G}_m)_X \xrightarrow{\ n\ } (\mathbb{G}_m)_X \longrightarrow 0 \] if \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) is invertible on \(X\).

Indeed, let \(u \in (\mathbb{G}_m)_X(U)\), \(U \longrightarrow X\) étale. We must find an étale covering \(\{ U_i \longrightarrow U \}\) of \(U\) such that \(u\) induces an \(n\)-th power on each \(U_i\). Since \(n\) is invertible on \(U\), the equation \[ T^n - u = 0 \] is "separable" over \(U\), i.e., \[ U' = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_U[T]/(T^n - u) \] is étale over \(U\). Since \(U' \longrightarrow U\) is surjective, it is covering, and \(u\) induces an \(n\)-th power on \(U'\); we are done.

Let us point out that when \(n\) is invertible on \(X\), \((\mu_n)_X\) is a locally constant sheaf, in fact locally isomorphic to the sheaf \((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_X\), and is constant in important cases. Kummer theory thus gives information about the cohomology of \(X\) with values in certain constant sheaves. In fact, by definition we have \[ H^0(X, (\mathbb{G}_m)_X) = \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}^*_X) , \] and for dimension \(1\) we have the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.3

("Hilbert's Theorem 90"): We have an isomorphism \[ H^1(X, (\mathbb{G}_m)_X) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Pic} X , \] where \(\operatorname{Pic} X\) is the group of classes of invertible sheaves on \(X\).

Proof. This means that the canonical morphism \[ H^1(X_{\text{zar}}, (\mathbb{G}_m)_X) \longrightarrow H^1(X_{\text{ét}}, (\mathbb{G}_m)_X) \] is bijective, which amounts to the same as saying that \[ R^1 \varepsilon_*(\mathbb{G}_m)_X = 0 \] where \(\varepsilon_*\) is the direct image for the obvious morphism of sites \(\varepsilon : X_{\text{ét}} \longrightarrow X_{\text{zar}}\) (VIII 4). We are therefore reduced to the case where \(X\) is affine. Since \(H^1\) can be computed by Čech (V 2.5), and since for a quasi-compact \(X\) it suffices to take quasi-compact coverings, this is an immediate consequence of descent theory for sheaves (cf. FGA 190, or SGA VIII 1).

Suppose \(X\) noetherian and without immersed component, and let \(x_j\) be the maximal points of \(X\). Let \(R_j\) be the artinian local ring of \(X\) at \(x_j\), and \(i_j : \operatorname{Spec} R_j \longrightarrow X\) the inclusion morphism.

We have a canonical injection \[ (\mathbb{G}_m)_X \longrightarrow \prod_j i_{j*}(\mathbb{G}_m)_{\operatorname{Spec} R_j} \] of sheaves on \(X_{\text{ét}}\) (resp. \(X_{\text{zar}}\)). The cokernel \(D\) is called the sheaf of Cartier divisors on \(X_{\text{ét}}\) (resp. \(X_{\text{zar}}\))(∗).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.4

Let \(X\) be noetherian and without immersed component, let \(\varepsilon : X_{\text{ét}} \longrightarrow X_{\text{zar}}\) be the canonical morphism of sites, and let \(D\) be the sheaf of Cartier divisors on \(X_{\text{ét}}\). Then \(\varepsilon_* D\) is the sheaf \(D_{\text{zar}}\) of Cartier divisors on \(X_{\text{zar}}\), and in particular one has: \[ H^0(X_{\text{ét}}, D) \approx H^0(X_{\text{zar}}, D_{\text{zar}}) . \]

Proof. If one applies \(\varepsilon_*\) to the exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow (\mathbb{G}_m)_X \longrightarrow \prod_j i_{j*}(\mathbb{G}_m)_{\operatorname{Spec} R_j} \longrightarrow D \longrightarrow 0 , \] one finds an exact sequence, since \(R^1 \varepsilon_*(\mathbb{G}_m)_X = 0\) (3.3), whence the first assertion.
In the case where \(X\) has a characteristic \(p \neq 0\), the following result will sometimes replace 3.2 for the study of \(p\)-torsion coefficients:

blocks.title: Artin-Schreier Theory
blocks.html:
Artin-Schreier Theory 3.5

We have the exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})_X \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X \xrightarrow{\ \wp\ } \mathcal{O}_X \longrightarrow 0 , \] if \(X\) is of characteristic \(p > 0\), where \(\wp\) is the morphism of additive groups defined by \(\wp(f) = f^p - f\).

The kernel of \(\wp\) is the sheaf of sections of \(\mathcal{O}_X\) which are locally in the prime field, hence is a constant sheaf. The morphism \(\wp\) is surjective for the étale topology because the equation \(T^p - T - a\) (\(a \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}_U)\)) is always "separable" in characteristic \(p\), i.e. defines an étale covering of \(U\). To apply this exact sequence, one will of course use (VII 4.2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.6

(i) Let \(X\) be a scheme and \(i : x \longrightarrow X\) the inclusion of a point. Then \[ H^1(X, i_*(\mathbb{Z})_x) = 0 \] where \((\mathbb{Z})_x\) is the "constant sheaf" (cf. 2.0) of value \(\mathbb{Z}\).

(ii) If \(X\) is irreducible and if for each geometric point \(\bar{x}\) of \(X\) the strict localization \(X_{\bar{x}}\) of \(X\) at \(\bar{x}\) is irreducible (one should say "\(X\) is geometrically unibranch" cf. EGA IV 18.8.14) then one has \[ H^1(X, \mathbb{Z}_X) = 0 . \]

Proof. (i) From the Leray spectral sequence \[ E_2^{pq} = H^p(X, R^q i_*(\mathbb{Z})_x) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(x, (\mathbb{Z})_x) \] one deduces an injection \(H^1(X, i_*(\mathbb{Z})_x) \longrightarrow H^1(x, (\mathbb{Z})_x)\). But since \(x = \operatorname{Spec} k(x)\) is the spectrum of a field, it is well known that \(H^1(x, (\mathbb{Z})_x) = 0\) (this follows from the fact that \(H^q(x, F)\) (\(q > 0\)) is in any case torsion (cf. VII 2.2 and CG), and from the exact sequences \(0 \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{\ n\ } \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}/n \longrightarrow 0\)), whence the result.

(ii) Let \(i : x \to X\) be the inclusion of the generic point of \(X\). One sees immediately that under the conditions of (ii) the canonical morphism \((\mathbb{Z})_X \longrightarrow i_*(\mathbb{Z})_x\) is bijective (the converse being moreover also true!), and (ii) is thus reduced to (i).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 3.7

In 3.6 (i) and (ii) one can replace \(\mathbb{Z}\) by any torsion-free abelian group. On the other hand, (ii) becomes false if one drops the hypothesis that \(X\) is geometrically unibranch, as one sees for example by taking for \(X\) an algebraic curve over a field \(K\), admitting an ordinary double point (carry out the computation of \(H^1(X, \mathbb{Z})\) in this case!)

footnotes.html: (∗) In EGA IV 21, one says simply "divisors" instead of "Cartier divisors".

pages.title: 4. The case of an algebraic curve

blocks.html: 4. The case of an algebraic curve

Let \(X\) be a noetherian scheme of dimension \(1\). Let \(R(X)\) be the ring of rational functions on \(X\), and \(i : \operatorname{Spec} R(X) \longrightarrow X\) the inclusion morphism. The ring \(R(X)\) is artinian, the product of the local rings of \(X\) at the maximal points, and one can use the results of (VIII 2).

Let \(F\) be an abelian sheaf on \(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)\) and consider the sheaves \(R^q i_* F\), \(q > 0\), on \(X\). It follows at once from VIII 5.2 that the stalk of \(R^q i_* F\) at a geometric point over a maximal point of \(X\) is zero. Since \(X\) is of dimension \(1\), such a sheaf is of a very special nature:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.1

Let \(X\) be noetherian and \(F\) a sheaf on \(X\). The following conditions are equivalent (a sheaf satisfying these conditions will be called a "skyscraper sheaf"):

(i) The stalk of \(F\), at every geometric point \(\bar{x}\) of \(X\) which is over a non-closed point \(x \in X\), is zero.

(ii) Each section \(s \in F(X')\) (\(X' \longrightarrow X\) étale of finite type) is zero, except at a finite number of closed points of \(X\).

(iii) One has \(F \approx \bigoplus_x i_{x*} i_x^* F\), where \(x\) runs through the set of closed points of \(X\) and where \(i_x : x \to X\) is the inclusion.

Proof. Suppose that (i) holds, and let \(z \in F(X')\) (\(X' \longrightarrow X\) étale of finite type). Then the support of \(z\) (VIII 6.6) is a closed subset of \(X'\) consisting of closed points, hence finite (\(X'\) being noetherian), whence (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii). The implication (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i) follows from the computation of stalks (VIII 3.9), and (iii) implies (i), for any family \((G_x)\) of sheaves on the closed points \(x\) of \(X\), the sheaf \(F = \bigoplus_x i_{x*}(G_x)\) on \(X\) satisfies (i), as follows from the fact that the stalk functors commute with direct sums, and that the support of \(i_{x*}(G_x)\) is obviously contained in \(\{ x \}\).

It remains to show that (ii) implies (iii). Consider the canonical morphism \[ F \longrightarrow \prod_x i_{x*} i_x^* F , \] \(x\) running through the set of closed points of \(X\). By (ii), it factors through \[ F \longrightarrow \bigoplus_x i_{x*} i_x^* F , \] which gives the sought morphism. We leave to the reader the verification of the fact that it is bijective.

Let us apply the lemma to the sheaf \(R^q i_* F\) introduced above: We have \[ R^q i_* F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \bigoplus_x i_{x*} i_x^*(R^q i_* F) \] (\(x\) running through the set of closed points of \(X\)). But by (VIII 5) the stalk of \(R^q i_* F\) at a geometric point \(\bar{x}\) of \(X\) is \[ (R^q i_* F)_{\bar{x}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(\operatorname{Spec} R(X_{\bar{x}}), F) \] where \(R(X_{\bar{x}}) \xrightarrow{\sim} R(X) \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_{X_{\bar{x}}}\), \(X_{\bar{x}}\) being the strict localization of \(X\) at \(\bar{x}\) (VIII 4), and where we also denote by \(F\) the sheaf induced by \(F\) on \(\operatorname{Spec} R(X_{\bar{x}})\). Suppose now that the residue field of every closed point \(x\) of \(X\) is separably closed. We shall then have (cf. also (VI. 1)) \[ \begin{aligned} H^p(X, R^q i_* F) &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^p\Big(X, \bigoplus_x i_{x*} i_x^*(R^q i_* F)\Big) \\ &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \bigoplus_x H^p(X, i_{x*} i_x^*(R^q i_* F)) \\ &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \bigoplus_x H^p(x, i_x^*(R^q i_* F)) \\ &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \begin{cases} \bigoplus_x H^q(\operatorname{Spec} R(X_x), F) & \text{if } p = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } p > 0 . \end{cases} \end{aligned} \]
We obtain the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2

Let \(X\) be a noetherian scheme of dimension \(1\), such that for every closed point \(x\) of \(X\), the residue field \(k(x)\) is sepa- rably closed. Let \(F\) be an abelian sheaf, on \(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)\) (where \(R(X) =\) ring of rational functions on \(X\)). Consider the Leray spectral sequence ( ). \[ E_2^{pq} = H^p(X, R^q i_* F) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Spec} R(X), F) . \] One has \[ E_2^{pq} = 0 \qquad \text{if } p \text{ and } q > 0 , \] \[ E_2^{0q} = \bigoplus_x H^q(\operatorname{Spec} R(X_x), F) \qquad \text{if } q > 0 , \] where \(x\) runs through the set of closed points of \(X\), and where \(X_x\) is the strict localization of \(X\) at the point \(x\).

The spectral sequence thus gives an exact sequence \[ \begin{aligned} 0 \longrightarrow H^1(X, i_* F) &\longrightarrow H^1(\operatorname{Spec} R(X), F) \longrightarrow \bigoplus_x H^1(\operatorname{Spec} R(X_x), F) \\ \longrightarrow H^2(X, i_* F) &\longrightarrow H^2(\operatorname{Spec} R(X), F) \longrightarrow \bigoplus_x H^2(\operatorname{Spec} R(X_x), F) \\ &\longrightarrow \cdots . \end{aligned} \]

Suppose now moreover that the \(\ell\)-cohomological dimension of \(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)\), for a given prime number \(\ell\), is at most equal to \(1\) (that is, that one has \(H^q(\operatorname{Spec} R(X), F) = 0\), \(q > 1\), for each sheaf \(F\) of \(\ell\)-torsion on \(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)\)). Let \(K^1, \ldots, K^m\) be the residue fields of the artinian ring \(R(X)\), i.e. the residue fields of the maximal points of \(X\). Taking into account the dictionary (VIII 2.1), the \(\ell\)-cohomological dimension of \(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)\) is \[ \operatorname{cd}_\ell(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)) = \sup_i \{ \operatorname{cd}_\ell(G(\bar{K}^i/K^i)) \} , \] where \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell(G)\) is the \(\ell\)-cohomological dimension of the profinite group \(G\) [cf. CG].

Each residue field \(K_x\) of \(R(\bar{X}(x))\), for a strict localization \(\bar{X}(x)\) of \(X\), is obviously identified with an (infinite) separable extension of one of the \(K^i\), whence \[ \operatorname{cd}_\ell(G(\bar{K}_x/K_x)) \leqslant \operatorname{cd}_\ell(G(\bar{K}^i/K^i)) \] by (CG II 4.1, Prop. 10). Hence the \(\ell\)-cohomological dimension \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell(\operatorname{Spec} R(\bar{X}(x)))\) is also \(\leqslant 1\).

Applying the exact sequence of 4.2 to an \(F\) of \(\ell\)-torsion, one finds \[ (4.3.1) \qquad \left\{ \begin{aligned} &0 \to H^1(X, i_* F) \to H^1(\operatorname{Spec} R(X), F) \to \\ &\qquad \bigoplus_x H^1(\operatorname{Spec} R(\bar{X}(x)), F) \to H^2(X, i_* F) \to 0 , \\ &H^q(X, i_* F) = 0 \quad \text{for } q > 2 . \end{aligned} \right. \]

Let us remark that the hypothesis that \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell(\operatorname{Spec} R(X))\) be \(\leqslant 1\) is satisfied if \(X\) is an algebraic curve over a separably closed field. (Tsen's Theorem [6, th.4.3]). Analogous exact sequences have been studied in this case by Ogg [2] and Šafarevič.

Suppose that \(\ell\) is invertible on \(X\) and take \(F = (\mathbb{G}_m)_{R(X)}\). Applying 3.3 and [CG, chap. I, prop. 12], one finds, still under the hypothesis that \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)) \leqslant 1\), \[ (4.4.1) \qquad \left\{ \begin{aligned} &H^1(\operatorname{Spec} R(X), \mathbb{G}_m) = 0 \\ &H^q(\operatorname{Spec} R(X), \mathbb{G}_m) \underset{\ell}{=} 0 \qquad q \geqslant 2 , \end{aligned} \right. \] where the \(\ell\) under the equality means that the group on the left-hand side, which is torsion in any case, has no \(\ell\)-torsion.

One has the same result if one replaces \(R(X)\) by \(R(\bar{X}(x))\). Since the sheaf \(\mathbb{G}_m\) on \(\operatorname{Spec} R(X)\) obviously induces the sheaf \(\mathbb{G}_m\) on \(\operatorname{Spec} R(\bar{X}(x))\), one deduces from 4.2 \[ (4.4.2) \qquad \left\{ \begin{aligned} &H^1(X, i_*(\mathbb{G}_m)_{R(X)}) = 0 \\ &H^q(X, i_*(\mathbb{G}_m)_{R(X)}) \underset{\ell}{=} 0 , \qquad \text{if } q > 1 . \end{aligned} \right. \]

But for every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), one sees thanks to 4.1 that the kernel \(P\) and cokernel \(Q\) of the canonical homomorphism \(F \longrightarrow i_* i^* F\) are "skyscraper sheaves", hence (since the residue fields at the closed points of \(X\) are assumed separably closed) one has \(H^i(X, P) = H^i(X, Q) = 0\) for \(i > 0\), which immediately implies, by the cohomology exact sequence, that \[ H^i(X, F) \longrightarrow H^i(X, i_* i^* F) \] is an isomorphism for \(i \geqslant 2\). Taking 4.4.2 into account, one concludes the relation \[ (4.5) \qquad H^i(X, \mathbb{G}_m) \underset{\ell}{=} 0 \qquad \text{for } i \geqslant 2 , \] valid when \(X\) is a noetherian prescheme of dimension \(1\), satisfying \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell(R(X)) \leqslant 1\), and whose residue fields at the closed points are separably closed. Taking into account Kummer theory (3.2) and (3.3), one concludes the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.6

Let \(X\) be noetherian of dimension \(1\), \(n\) an integer which is invertible on \(X\), suppose that \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell(R(X)) \leqslant 1\) for each prime number \(\ell\) which divides \(n\), and that for every closed point \(x\) of \(X\), the residue field \(k(x)\) is separably closed. Then one has \[ H^q(X, (\mu_n)_X) = 0 \quad \text{if } q > 2 , \] and the cohomology for \(q \leqslant 2\) is given by the exact sequence \[ \begin{aligned} 0 \longrightarrow H^0(X, (\mu_n)_X) &\longrightarrow \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}^*_X) \xrightarrow{\ n\ } \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}^*_X) \longrightarrow \\ H^1(X, (\mu_n)_X) &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic} X \xrightarrow{\ n\ } \operatorname{Pic} X \longrightarrow H^2(X, (\mu_n)_X) \longrightarrow 0 . \end{aligned} \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.7

Let \(X\) be a complete connected curve over a separably closed field \(k\), of characteristic prime to \(n\). Then one has \[ H^0(X, (\mu_n)_X) \simeq \mu_n(k) , \] \[ H^1(X, (\mu_n)_X) \simeq {}_n(\operatorname{Pic} X) = \text{set of elements of } \operatorname{Pic} X \text{ whose order divides } n , \] \[ H^2(X, (\mu_n)_X) \simeq (\operatorname{Pic} X)/n \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^c , \] where \(c\) is the set of irreducible components of \(X\).

For the last assertion, let us "recall" that the "Picard scheme" [TDTE V] of such an \(X/\operatorname{Spec} k\) admits a decomposition \[ (4.8) \qquad 0 \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}_{X/k} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}^c \longrightarrow 0 \] where \(A\) is a connected algebraic group over \(\operatorname{Spec} k\). But the map "multiplication by \(n\)" in such an \(A\) is étale, hence surjective for the points with values in \(k\). It follows that one has \[ {}_n(\operatorname{Pic} X) \approx {}_n(A(k)) \] and \[ (\operatorname{Pic} X)/n \approx (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^c . \]

If \(X\) is smooth over \(\operatorname{Spec} k\), so that the Jacobian \(A\) is an abelian variety, the group \({}_n(\operatorname{Pic} X)\) is isomorphic to \((\mathbb{Z}/n)^{2g}\), where \(g\) is the genus of \(X\). Of course, one also has \(\mu_n(k) \approx \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\), hence the ranks of the cohomology groups as \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules are \(1\), \(2g\), \(1\), which is the result one should expect.
5. The trace method

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(f : X' \longrightarrow X\) an étale covering, and \(F\) a sheaf on \(X\). Then the adjunction formulas give a restriction morphism \[ F \xrightarrow{\ \text{res}\ } f_* f^* F . \] Since \(f\) is finite, one has \(H^q(X, f_* f^* F) \simeq H^q(X', f^* F)\), whence a morphism, also called restriction: \[ (5.1.1) \qquad H^q(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \text{res}\ } H^q(X', f^* F) , \] which is moreover the obvious morphism. But in the case \(f\) étale one also has another morphism, called the trace morphism \[ (5.1.2) \qquad f_* f^* F \xrightarrow{\ \text{tr}\ } F , \] which gives morphisms on cohomology \[ (5.1.3) \qquad H^q(X', f^* F) \xrightarrow{\ \text{tr}\ } H^q(X, F) . \] The trace morphism is characterized by the following two properties:
(i) It is of local character for the étale topology.
(ii) If \(X'\) is the disjoint sum of \(d\) copies of \(X\), so that \(f_* f^* F \simeq F^d\), the trace is the sum map \(F^d \longrightarrow F\).
Uniqueness is trivial from (i), (ii) since every étale covering is locally constant. Having uniqueness, existence follows by the usual descent argument.
From (ii) one deduces the following formula: \[ (5.1.4) \qquad \operatorname{tr}\circ\operatorname{res} : F \longrightarrow F \text{ is multiplication by the local degree of } f . \]
If the degree is a constant \(d\), one deduces that the morphism \(\operatorname{tr}\circ\operatorname{res} : H^q(X, F) \longrightarrow H^q(X, F)\) is multiplication by \(d\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2

Let \(f : X' \longrightarrow X\) be an étale covering of constant degree \(d\). If \(F\) is a sheaf of \(r\)-torsion on \(X\) with \((r,d)=1\), then \(H^q(X', f^* F) = 0\) implies that \(H^q(X, F) = 0\).
Indeed, multiplication by \(d\) induces an isomorphism of \(F\), hence an isomorphism on cohomology. If the latter isomorphism factors through zero, one has \(H^q(X, F) = 0\).

Let now \(i : U \longrightarrow X\) be an immersion, \(f : U' \longrightarrow U\) an étale covering of degree \(d\), and suppose \(f\) induced by a finite morphism \(g : X' \longrightarrow X\) by base change, i.e. we then have the cartesian diagram \[ \xymatrix{ U' \ar[r]^{i'} \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[d]^{g} \\ U \ar[r]_{i} & X } \] Let \(F\) be a sheaf on \(U\). We have \[ \xymatrix{ F \ar[r]^-{\text{res}} \ar@/_1.8pc/[rr]_{d} & f_* f^* F \ar[r]^-{\text{tr}} & F } , \] hence, since \(i_* f_* = g_* i'_*\), \[ (5.3) \qquad \xymatrix{ i_* F \ar[r]^-{\text{res}} \ar@/_1.8pc/[rr]_{d} & g_* i'_* f^* F \ar[r]^-{\text{tr}} & i_* F } , \] and since \(i_! f_! \simeq g_* i'_!\) (follows e.g. from (VIII 5.5)), \[ (5.4) \qquad \xymatrix{ i_! F \ar[r]^-{\text{res}} \ar@/_1.8pc/[rr]_{d} & g_* i'_! f^* F \ar[r]^-{\text{tr}} & i_! F } , \] whence \[ (5.3') \qquad \xymatrix{ H^q(X, i_* F) \ar[r]^-{\text{res}} \ar@/_1.8pc/[rr]_{d'} & H^q(X', i'_* f^* F) \ar[r]^-{\text{tr}} & H^q(X, i_* F) } \] and \[ (5.4') \qquad \xymatrix{ H^q(X, i_! F) \ar[r]^-{\text{res}} \ar@/_1.8pc/[rr]_{d} & H^q(X', i'_! f^* F) \ar[r]^-{\text{tr}} & H^q(X, i_! F) } ; \]
From (5.4) one deduces the following corollaries:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5

Let \(X\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme, \(\ell \in \mathbb{P}\), and let \(H\) be a semi-exact functor with values in \((\mathrm{Ab})\), defined on the category of \(\ell\)-sheaves on \(X\), and compatible with filtered inductive limits. The following assertions are equivalent:

(i) \(H = 0\).

(ii) \(H(f_* i_!(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)) = 0\) for each \(f : Y \longrightarrow X\) finite, and each open \(i : U \longrightarrow Y\) of \(Y\), such that \(U\) is of finite presentation over \(X\). If \(X\) is noetherian, one may even restrict to taking \(Y\) integral.

Proof. By 2.7.2 and 2.5 it suffices to verify \(H(F) = 0\) for \(F\) of the form \(F = i_! G\), where \(i : U \longrightarrow X\) is the inclusion of a subscheme of \(X\) of finite presentation over \(X\), and where \(G\) is an "isotrivial" locally constant \(\ell\)-sheaf on \(U\). Let \(U'' \longrightarrow U\) be a principal covering, with group \(g\), such that \(g\) becomes constant on \(U''\). Let \(A\) be the \(\ell\)-group of the values of \(G\) on \(U''\). The group \(g\) acts on \(A\), and this action determines the structure of \(G\). Let \(h\) be a Sylow \(\ell\)-subgroup of \(g\), and let \(U' = U''/h\) be the covering of \(U\) corresponding to \(h\). The degree \(d\) of \(U'\) over \(U\) is prime to \(\ell\). Let us take an extension of \(f : U' \longrightarrow U\) to a finite morphism \(g : X' \longrightarrow X\), which always exists (EGA IV 8.12.6), and let \(i' : U' \longrightarrow X'\) be the inclusion. Applying 5.4 and the fact that \(d\) is prime to \(\ell\), we reduce to showing that \(H(g_* i'_! f^* G) = 0\).

But it is well known that the only abelian \(\ell\)-torsion group which is simple for an action of an \(\ell\)-group \(h\) is \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell\) with trivial action, and it follows that there exists a filtration of \(A\) as an \(h\)-module, whose successive quotients are isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell\) with trivial action. This filtration gives a corresponding filtration of \(f^* G\), and it therefore suffices, in order to show that \(H(g_* i'_! f^* G) = 0\), to show that \(H(g_* i'_! \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\), whence the result.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.6

Let \(X\) be a noetherian scheme, \(\ell \in \mathbb{P}\), and \(\varphi\) a function with values in \(\mathbb{N}\), defined on the set of integral schemes finite over \(X\). Suppose \(\varphi(Y_1) \leqslant \varphi(Y_2)\) whenever there exists an \(X\)-morphism \(Y_1 \longrightarrow Y_2\), and that the inequality is strict if \(Y_1\) is a closed subscheme of \(Y_2\), distinct from \(Y_2\). For every \(Y\) finite over \(X\), set \(\varphi(Y) = \sup_i \varphi(Y_i)\), where the \(Y_i\) are the irreducible components of \(Y\), equipped with the induced reduced structure. Then the following assertions are equivalent:

(i) For each \(Y\) finite over \(X\) and each \(\ell\)-sheaf \(F\) on \(Y\) one has \(H^q(Y, F) = 0\) if \(q > \varphi(\operatorname{Supp} F)\).

(ii) For each \(Y\) integral finite over \(X\) one has \(H^q(Y, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) if \(q > \varphi(Y)\).

Proof. Suppose that (ii) holds. One can apply the preceding proposition to each \(H^q\), taking into account that cohomology commutes with inductive limits and with direct images by finite morphisms, and one thus reduces, for the verification of (i), to the case \(Y\) integral finite over \(X\), and \(F\) of the form \(i_!(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_U\), where \(i : U \longrightarrow X\) is a nonempty open.

But one has an exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow i_!(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_U \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_Y \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_Z \longrightarrow 0 \] where \(Z = Y-U\), so \(Z \neq Y\). Making an induction on the value of \(\varphi\), we may assume that \(H^q(Z, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) for \(q > \varphi(Y)-1\), whence \(H^q(Y, i_!(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)) = 0\) for \(q > \varphi(Y)\) thanks to the cohomology exact sequence.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7

Let \(X\) be an algebraic curve over a separably closed field \(k\) of characteristic different from \(\ell\), \(\ell \in \mathbb{P}\). Then the coho- mology of \(X\) in a sheaf \(F\) of \(\ell\)-torsion is zero in dimension \(> 2\). If \(X\) is affine, the cohomology is zero in dimension \(> 1\).

Set, for \(Y\) finite integral over \(X\), \(\varphi(Y) = 2 \dim Y\) (resp. \(\varphi(Y) = \dim Y\) if \(X\), hence \(Y\), is affine). By 5.6 it suffices to show that \(H^q(Y, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) if \(q > \varphi(Y)\). But this is trivial if \(\dim Y = 0\). It therefore remains to show that \(H^q(Y, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) if \(q > 2\) (resp. if \(q > 1\) in the affine case) for an integral curve \(Y\). Since \((\mathbb{Z}/\ell)_Y \simeq (\mu_\ell)_Y\), this is a consequence of 4.6 for \(q > 2\).

Suppose \(X\) affine. Since radicial extensions do not affect cohomology (VIII 1.1), we reduce to the case where \(k\) is algebraically closed. Let \(f : X' \longrightarrow X\) be the normalization of \(X\), which is a finite morphism and an isomorphism outside a finite set of points, say \(S\). We have an exact sequence of sheaves on \(X\) \[ 0 \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/n)_X \longrightarrow f_*(\mathbb{Z}/n)_{X'} \longrightarrow \mathscr{E} \longrightarrow 0 , \] where \(\mathscr{E}\) is concentrated on \(S\), hence \(H^q(X, \mathscr{E}) = 0\) for \(q > 0\). We reduce, by (VIII 5.6), to showing that \[ H^q(X, f_*(\mathbb{Z}/n)_{X'}) \simeq H^q(X', \mathbb{Z}/n) = 0 \] if \(q > 1\), that is, to the case \(X\) normal. One can also obviously assume \(X\) connected. Let \(i : X \longrightarrow \bar{X}\) be an open immersion with \(\bar{X}\) complete and nonsingular. Since \(X\) is affine, at least one point of \(\bar{X}\) is missing, and one sees immediately that consequently the morphism \[ A(k) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic} X \] is surjective, where \(A\) is the Jacobian of \(\bar{X}\) (cf. 4.8). Since \(A(k)\) is divisible by \(\ell \neq \operatorname{car} k\), the same holds for \(\operatorname{Pic} X\), whence \(H^2(X, \mu_\ell) = 0\) by 4.6, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.8

Let us point out, for later reference, that the reasoning of 5.5 in fact establishes the following result: Let \(X\) be a quasi- compact and quasi-separated scheme, \(\ell\) a prime number, \(C\) a strictly full subcategory of the category of constructible abelian sheaves of \(\ell\)-torsion, stable under direct factors and under extensions. Suppose that for each finite morphism \(f : Y \longrightarrow X\) and each open \(i : U \longrightarrow Y\) of \(Y\) which is of finite presentation over \(X\), one has \(f_*(i_!(\underline{\mathbb{Z}/\ell\,\mathbb{Z}})_U) \in C\). Then \(C\) contains all constructible sheaves of \(\ell\)-torsion.
